tldr: Aegis Space Law is a Washington DC boutique founded in 2020, Chambers Band 3 for space, covering trade compliance, FAA, FCC, NOAA, government contracting, and formation, with rare published pricing: quarterly subscriptions from $5,000 (about 12 hours) to $44,000 (about 74 hours), an effective rate of roughly $390 to $595 per hour. That buys legal counsel by the hour. It does not buy a filing pipeline. Invariant is the execution alternative: agents draft FCC, FAA, NOAA, ITU, and export control filings with every answer traced to its source rule, and a forward-deployed licensing engineer owns the work end to end. sections.heading: What Aegis Space Law is
paragraphs: Aegis Space Law is a boutique law firm in Washington DC, founded in 2020, that works exclusively on commercial space. Its seven practice areas: US trade compliance (ITAR, EAR, OFAC), launch and reentry licensing before the FAA, telecommunications before the FCC and ITU, remote sensing before NOAA, business formation and fundraising, government contracting, and commercial contracts. Chambers USA ranks the firm Band 3 for space nationwide in its 2025 and 2026 guides, with founding partner Bailey Reichelt individually ranked. The firm is also a Legal Connect Partner of NATO DIANA.

Aegis has done two things most law firms refuse to do. It publishes its prices, and it ships free tools: a Space Regulatory Calculator, launched in June 2024, that tells a startup which federal licenses apply to its mission, and a US export risk assessment tool. Both are genuinely useful, and both are the reason the firm punches above its size in visibility among space startups.

sections.heading: Aegis pricing, with the effective hourly math
paragraphs: Aegis sells quarterly subscriptions in two plans. The basic plan covers formation, trade compliance, and contracts. The comprehensive plan adds FCC, SEC, NOAA, and FAA licensing work. Flat-rate projects and traditional hourly billing are offered alongside.

Run the arithmetic on the published tiers and the subscription is hourly billing with a cleaner label: roughly $390 to $450 per effective hour on the basic plan and $540 to $595 on the comprehensive plan. That is materially cheaper than big law, where the median partner rate at the 100 largest US firms passed $1,000 per hour in 2025. It is still a meter running on hours, and licensing programs consume hours relentlessly.
bullets: Basic plan: $5,000 per quarter for about 12 hours, rising through $9,000 (20 hours), $13,300 (30 hours), and $18,000 (42 hours) to $28,800 for about 74 hours
Comprehensive plan (adds FCC, SEC, NOAA, FAA): $6,500 to $44,000 per quarter across the same hour tiers
Consultation tiers: $2,500 (basic) or $3,250 (comprehensive) for strategy sessions with no deliverables
Effective rates from the published numbers: about $390 to $450 per hour basic, $540 to $595 comprehensive

sections.heading: What a legal subscription buys, and what it does not
paragraphs: A subscription buys access to lawyers: answers to legal questions, contract review, classification opinions, and drafting help, metered in hours per quarter. For a company that needs episodic counsel, that is a fair product at a fair price.

What it does not buy is a filing pipeline. A single FCC space station application is a comprehensive technical proposal under 47 CFR 25.114: Form 312, Schedule S orbital and RF data, an orbital debris showing with hard numerical thresholds, and narrative exhibits that must stay consistent with the ITU filing, any NOAA application, and the export control posture, through every design revision. A first-time commercial licensing campaign burns through a 74-hour quarterly tier before the first regulator question comes back. The work is not legal judgment most of the way down: it is drafting, requirement tracing, cross-document consistency, and deadline management, at volume.

sections.heading: Aegis vs Invariant, honestly
paragraphs: These are different species, and the comparison is only useful if it says so plainly. Aegis is a law firm: licensed attorneys, legal advice, attorney-client privilege, opinions you can rely on in an enforcement posture. Invariant is a licensing platform: agents draft the FCC, FAA, NOAA, ITU, and export control filings with every answer traced to the rule that requires it, and a forward-deployed licensing engineer owns the work end to end, through submission packaging and regulator correspondence. Invariant is not a law firm and does not provide legal advice.

The economics differ the same way. A firm meters hours against a clock, so cost scales with the volume of work. Invariant runs the pipeline itself, so the drafting grind does not return to a partner's meter every quarter. And the operating models differ: a firm answers when asked, while the platform monitors continuously, which is what the moment demands: the FCC adopted its Part 100 overhaul in July 2026 and the transition rules will keep moving under every operator's feet for the next year.
bullets: Legal advice and privilege: Aegis yes, Invariant no, by design
Who does the drafting: Aegis attorneys bill hours for it; Invariant agents draft and an engineer owns the output
Pricing: Aegis $5,000 to $44,000 per quarter for 12 to 74 hours; Invariant platform pricing, not metered by the hour
Software: Aegis offers a free regulatory calculator; Invariant is the platform, with requirement tracing, filing drafting, and continuous rule-change monitoring
Best for: Aegis for counsel, opinions, formation, and enforcement-sensitive questions; Invariant for running the multi-agency filing pipeline
Compatible: many teams keep a firm for privilege and run the filings on Invariant

sections.heading: When Aegis is the right call
paragraphs: Use a law firm for the work only a law firm can do. Company formation and fundraising documents. ITAR commodity jurisdiction and classification opinions you may need to rely on as a defense. Voluntary disclosures and enforcement inquiries, where privilege matters from the first conversation. Novel legal interpretations without precedent. If you want that from a team that only does space, at published prices well under big law rates, Aegis is a credible choice, and the Chambers ranking backs that up.

sections.heading: When Invariant is the right call
paragraphs: Use Invariant when the problem is the pipeline: getting a constellation, launch campaign, or remote sensing mission through FCC, FAA, NOAA, ITU, and export control filings that must stay mutually consistent for years, on deadlines that do not move. Agents draft every filing with citations back to source rules, flag inconsistencies across workstreams, and track regulatory changes like the Part 100 transition as they land. A forward-deployed licensing engineer owns the outcome: not a memo about the filing, the filing. The same model runs Invariant's nuclear licensing practice, which no space law boutique offers.

faqs.question: What is Aegis Space Law?
faqs.answer: A boutique law firm in Washington DC, founded in 2020, that works exclusively on commercial space: trade compliance (ITAR, EAR, OFAC), FAA launch and reentry licensing, FCC and ITU telecommunications, NOAA remote sensing, government contracting, business formation, and commercial contracts. Chambers USA ranks it Band 3 for space nationwide in 2025 and 2026.

faqs.question: How much does Aegis Space Law cost?
faqs.answer: Aegis publishes quarterly subscription pricing: a basic plan from $5,000 (about 12 hours) to $28,800 (about 74 hours) covering formation, trade compliance, and contracts, and a comprehensive plan from $6,500 to $44,000 that adds FCC, SEC, NOAA, and FAA licensing. That works out to roughly $390 to $595 per effective hour. Flat-rate projects and hourly billing are also offered.

faqs.question: Is Aegis Space Law a good firm?
faqs.answer: By the observable evidence, yes for what it sells: Chambers USA ranks it Band 3 for space nationwide, founding partner Bailey Reichelt is individually ranked, it publishes its prices, and its free Space Regulatory Calculator is genuinely useful to startups. It is a law firm selling metered hours of counsel; whether that fits depends on whether your problem is legal questions or filing execution.

faqs.question: What is the best alternative to Aegis Space Law?
faqs.answer: It depends on the job. For legal counsel from a larger bench, Chambers ranks Hogan Lovells Cadwalader and Milbank in Band 1 and Akin, Cooley, Greenberg Traurig, and Wiley in Band 2. For the recurring filing pipeline itself, the alternative is Invariant: agents draft FCC, FAA, NOAA, ITU, and export control filings with every answer traced to its source rule, and a forward-deployed licensing engineer owns the work end to end. No FCC rule requires filings to come from an attorney.

faqs.question: Aegis Space Law vs Invariant: which should we use?
faqs.answer: Different tools. Aegis is a law firm: legal advice, privilege, opinions, metered in subscription hours at an effective $390 to $595 per hour. Invariant is a licensing platform: agents plus a forward-deployed licensing engineer who run the multi-agency filing pipeline end to end, without an hourly meter. Invariant is not a law firm. Teams with both needs use both: counsel for privilege-sensitive questions, Invariant for the filings.

faqs.question: Do we need a space law firm to get licensed at all?
faqs.answer: No. No FCC rule requires an attorney to prepare or file a satellite application: the applicant signs and files its own Form 312 through ICFS. ITAR registration is likewise filed by the company, and export licenses are signed by an Empowered Official who must be a company employee. Law firms matter for enforcement, disputes, deals, and opinions, not because the filings legally require them.
